## What changes at 10x

Horn's tree-merge ordering costs 0.78 ms at 209 tasks and 1.24 ms at 2090 tasks: its cost is a sort of the tasks plus a merge loop over the damaged zones, and the synthetic replication keeps the same 73 damaged zones, so ordering is not the bottleneck at either size. The exact objective evaluation grows from 0.83 ms to 4.14 ms per call and a full adjacent-swap pass from 0.16 s (measured) to 8.65 s (projected), so the swap pass is the quadratic part: the app's setting (swap pass capped at 1,500 evaluations, 1 s time ceiling) fits 1,204 evaluations (about 5.8 passes, 0.96% gain) at 209 tasks but only 218 evaluations (0.10 of a pass, stopped by the solver's 1 s time ceiling at 218 of the 1,500 capped evaluations) at 2090. At 209 tasks the descent ran to convergence in 8.70 s (11,648 evaluations, about 56 passes) for a 2.24% gain over the Horn order; at 10x one pass alone exceeds the interactive budget, so the app would show the Horn order with the pass truncated, which is what the evaluation cap and the time ceiling already do today. On this machine the 1 s ceiling, not the 1,500-evaluation cap, ends the pass on the largest demo circuit (reaching the cap needs about 1.24 s at the measured evaluation cost, projected), so the displayed schedule for this circuit is machine-dependent here; a faster machine reaches the cap and shows a slightly different, deterministic schedule. Simulated mode runs 20 Horn-only solves plus one capped solve: 2.58 s at 1x and 4.56 s at 3x on this circuit (mean 184 and 540 tasks per draw), against 1.21 s for the Observed set; the cost is per circuit, so a 10x territory means 10x as many independent journeys of this size, not one journey 10x as slow. The nearest-premise lookup is a linear scan (0.58 ms over 16,145 premises) that grows with the premise count; a spatial index removes that.

Three modeling points matter more than the runtimes. Per-circuit sharding: every circuit is its own protective-zone tree with its own damage set, so a territory is a sum of independent solves that run in parallel and cache per scenario. Shared crew pool: the prototype dedicates crews to one circuit; in a real storm a shared pool is allocated across circuits with travel between them (the ILM folds travel into task hours), which turns per-circuit ordering into a territory-wide assignment problem. Tie switches: circuits can be back-fed through normally-open tie switches, so service for a group becomes the earlier of two paths instead of one AND-chain; that breaks the out-tree assumption Horn's optimality rests on and needs an explicit switching step in the schedule.
